title: Tuba players he admired: Coon-Sanders, Isham Jones and Slim Waters
summary: He recalls tuba players in the Middle West bands and Slim Waters in Cleveland, who played tuba like a trumpet; Sweets Edison was then in Chester Clark's band.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Besides Braud and Eddie Cole, who else impressed you? Who else did you hear that you really remembered play bass?

Well, during that time I was also listening to tubas. Because they still hadn't discontinued the use of tubas in bands. I can remember listening to bands from the Middle West. There was a band called Coon Saunders' band, and they had a marvelous tuba player. I don't know whether it was Coon or Saunders, but anyway, the band really featured the tuba -- which all of the bands did at that time. Then there was the Isham Jones band, who I listened to. He had a great tuba player. I never did find out his name.
But there was also another tuba player whose name I do remember, who I first saw in Cleveland at the same time I met Sweets Edison. His name was Slim Waters. He was a
Black tuba player. It was a funny thing about him, he switched from tuba to trumpet, which was really a strange thing. But he played Jazz just like guys did on trumpets at that time.

On tuba, yes. And I think he would have been naturally part of my inspiration, too. Although I thought of the tuba principally at that time as a rhythm instrument, and only later did I begin to get into the melodic thing. That's not quite true, because I do remember when I was in school picking out melodies. "Stardust" was one. And I used to out on the campus by myself and play these things. This was before I even heard Slim Waters, who was phenomenal. He later became the President or something of a local in Philadelphia. I think he has left us now. But that was another one of my inspirations.
Did he play melodically on the tuba?
Yes, he played melodically, but he mostly played just Jazz. My teacher used to call it "hokum." But he played the tuba just like guys played trumpets. He had that facility even way back there.
Did he play with anybody's band that you know of?

Yeah, he played with a guy...I think it was Chester Clark's band. That's the band that Sweets was playing with. This is before Sweets ever went to Kansas City and joined the Jeter-Pillars band. You might have heard of that.
Because I told you when I first met Sweets, he was only 17. So yeah, that's part of something I remembered since our last conversation.
